hook: The persecutor turned apostle, who carried Christianity across the Roman world.

pages.x: Saul was a Jew from Tarsus, in what is now Turkey, and a Roman citizen. He trained as a Pharisee in Jerusalem and made tents for a living. He hunted down the followers of Jesus, and stood by approving as the first Christian martyr, Stephen, was stoned to death.

Riding to Damascus to arrest Christians, Saul was struck to the ground by a blinding light and heard a voice: "Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?" Blind for three days, he was healed and baptised. A "road to Damascus" moment still means a sudden change of heart.

pages.t: Over the wall in a basket
pages.x: He began to preach about Jesus in Damascus, and his old allies plotted to kill him. They watched the city gates day and night, so his friends lowered him down the outside of the city wall in a basket, after dark.

Now called Paul, he made three great journeys, perhaps 16,000 kilometres on foot and by ship, founding churches across Asia Minor and Greece: at Ephesus, Corinth, Philippi and Thessalonica. He insisted that non-Jews could become Christians without following Jewish law.

He wrote letters to the churches he had founded; thirteen books of the New Testament carry his name. One to the Corinthians holds his most famous words: "Love is patient, love is kind... And now these three remain: faith, hope and love. But the greatest of these is love."

Arrested in Jerusalem, he used his right as a Roman citizen to be judged by the emperor. Sailing to Rome as a prisoner, he was shipwrecked on Malta. In Rome he lived two years under guard, and tradition says he was beheaded there under Nero.
pages.img: Basilica of Saint Paul Outside the Walls

pages.x: Paul did more than anyone to turn a small Jewish movement into a faith open to every people. His letters are the oldest Christian writings and have shaped Christian belief ever since.
